Concepts

Capabilities and grants

A plugin can use only the parts of the host that it asks for. It lists the capabilities it needs in its manifest, one list per side. The user grants them when a package is installed or first activated. For bundled plugins the kernel grants everything up to the manifest ceiling, except the high-risk capabilities.

This page covers the grant syntax, the full capability surface, the tiers and the review dialog, what happens to an import that is granted, declined or never requested, the always-granted set, revocation and the error codes.

You will need

  • A manifest with a capabilities object. See Packages and manifests.
  • The server, client and scene sides. See Worlds and sides.
  • The Rust SDK (ilium-plugin-sdk) or the TypeScript SDK (@ilium/plugin-sdk). Both expose the granted list in the activation context. See Rust SDK and TypeScript SDK.

Grant syntax

A grant is a name, optionally followed by a colon and an argument. The first colon separates the name from the argument. Later colons belong to the argument.

grant    = name [ ":" argument ]
name     = segment *( "." segment )      segment = [a-z][a-z0-9-]*
argument = 1*char                         everything after the first colon

The grants commands.invoke, fs.read, fs.write, fs.watch, http, process.run, services.use, services.provide, messages.peer, topics.subscribe and http-api.route require an argument. Every other grant takes no argument, and tree.read:x is a manifest error. A service name has no version. The grant services.use:ilium:inference/provider has the name services.use and the argument ilium:inference/provider.

The manifest holds one list per side under capabilities. The scene side uses the key scene:

"capabilities": {
  "server": ["tree.read", "fs.read:project", "http:api.example.com", "http:*.example.org"],
  "client": ["ui.panels", "panes.read"],
  "scene": []
}

Grants are per side. A server grant does not apply to the client side, and each side keeps its own list.

Extended grants

The grants below cover the wider kernel surface: tree restructuring, pane lifecycle, terminal and agent data, chrome, sessions, inference and process control. Eleven of them are high risk and always need an explicit grant, even for a T1 bundled plugin: terminal.history, terminal.input-lock, terminal.raw-input, panes.lifecycle, tree.restructure, sessions.cross, process.long-lived, agent.transcript, settings.read-kernel:api, settings.write-kernel:<tab> and panes.create-command:<program>. The grant gpu.kernels is unstable and exists only in development builds. Both extensions.* grants take exactly one global point id and refuse wildcards (manifest.grant-wildcard). extensions.contribute is high risk only for a point that declares risk: "high"; the review dialog then shows a warning. Four argument forms are worth knowing: http:setting:<key> (the host comes from one of the plugin's own settings, and the user confirms a changed host before the first request), fs.read:agent-sessions:gemini with fs.read:agent-config:gemini, fs.read:agent-config:antigravity, and settings.read-kernel:<kernel-tab-id> (argument required, no wildcard).

New grant Page

The always-granted set needs no entry in the manifest. See Always granted.

Wildcards and scopes

  • commands.invoke:<pattern> takes an exact global id, <plugin-id>/* for all commands of one plugin, or a bare * for all commands (H). A * never crosses /.
  • http:<host> takes an exact host, *.<domain> for any subdomain at any depth (not the bare domain), and an optional port. localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] allow plain HTTP. A bare * is refused.
  • topics.subscribe:<pattern> takes an exact topic, <prefix>/* or a bare *. Exact and prefix patterns are normal risk; only the bare * is high risk (H).
  • process.run:* is refused with manifest.grant-wildcard. process.run:sh is valid and H.
  • messages.peer:<plugin-id> takes one exact plugin id and no wildcard.
  • extensions.provide and extensions.contribute take one exact <plugin-id>/<point> and no wildcard. There is no extensions.contribute-any. List each point.

File scopes are the argument of fs.read, fs.write and fs.watch:

  • project is the project folder. It excludes the project's .ilium folder.
  • worktrees is the project's Git worktrees. fs.write:worktrees is H.
  • picked is each path the user chose in fs.pick.
  • data and cache are the plugin's own folders. Their read and write grants are always granted.
  • package is the plugin's own package. It is always readable and never watchable.
  • agent-sessions:<agent> holds transcripts and is H. It is read only.
  • agent-config:<agent> holds agent configuration. Writes are H.
  • minecraft-saves is the platform's saves folder.
  • path:<template> is a path template. It starts with a placeholder ({home}, {config}, {data}, {cache}, {project}, {worktrees}) or with a literal absolute path. A literal path is always H. The template ends with a name or with /**. A * anywhere else is refused.

Tiers and the review dialog

The kernel grants capabilities differently depending on the tier of the package.

Tier Source Grants
T1 First-party component embedded in the release The manifest ceiling is granted automatically, except H capabilities.
T2 Package signed by a key the user trusts The review dialog shows each capability. The user's choices are remembered.
T3 Unsigned local or development package The same review dialog, with a persistent development badge.

Install of a T2 or T3 package shows the review dialog. The plugin installs with the grants that the user leaves checked. H rows start unchecked. A declined row is dimmed and its grant is absent from the granted list.

For a T1 bundled plugin, activation starts without its H capabilities. The first activation shows one prompt per plugin, Plugin <name> asks for: <list>, with the buttons Allow selected and Not now. Not now asks again at the next server start, at most three times, and then never again. The user can grant the capability at any time from Settings > Plugins.

There is no prompt per call. A grant stays in force until it is revoked. The dialog below is drawn at 72 columns for a signed notes package.

Declined, unrequested and granted

The kernel links each import to one of three targets. The diagram shows them side by side.

  • Granted. The import works as its API page describes.
  • Declined. The import links to a stub. Functions with a result return not-permitted, and the plugin keeps running. Some functions have no error result, so they return a value instead. clipboard read-text and location current return none. plugins.list returns an empty list. A declined http-api.route answers 404 Not Found. A declined topic subscription delivers no events and returns no error. A refused call is written to the plugin log.
  • Not requested. The manifest never asked for the capability, so the import traps. The manifest and the code disagree, which is a plugin bug. The trap ends the instance and the kernel logs it.

Always granted

Every plugin has these without a request, and it need not list them: log, clock, timers, storage for its own buckets, settings for its own values, codec, read access to its package, read and write access to its own data and cache folders, messages between its own two sides, and ui.invalidate for the views it contributes. A manifest without capabilities behaves exactly like "capabilities": {}.

Reading the granted list

The activation context carries granted, the list of capabilities that were actually granted. A plugin should read it on every activation, because a revocation changes it. The example below hides the file feature when the project grant is missing and keeps the rest of the plugin working. The grant list is a hint, not a guarantee. A call can still return not-permitted or revoked.

Rust

use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{fs, log::{self, Level}};

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Notes;

impl Lifecycle for Notes {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if context.granted.iter().any(|grant| grant == "fs.read:project") {
            task::spawn(load_readme());
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, _reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        None
    }
}

impl Handler for Notes {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

async fn load_readme() {
    let path = FsPath { scope: "project".into(), path: "README.md".into() };
    match fs::read_all(path).await {
        Ok(bytes) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("README has {} bytes", bytes.len())),
        Err(error) if error.code == ErrorCode::NotPermitted => {
            log::log(Level::Warn, "project files are not granted");
        }
        Err(error) => log::log(Level::Error, &format!("README read failed: {}", error.message)),
    }
}

TypeScript

import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { readAll } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

async function loadReadme(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    const bytes = await readAll({ scope: 'project', path: 'README.md' });
    log('info', `README has ${bytes.length} bytes`);
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PluginError && error.code === 'not-permitted') {
      log('warn', 'project files are not granted');
      return;
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate(context) {
    if (context.granted.includes('fs.read:project')) {
      loadReadme().catch((error) => log('error', `README read failed: ${String(error)}`));
    }
  },
  onEvents(): Submission[] {
    return [];
  },
});

Changing grants

  • Revocation. The user revokes a grant in Settings > Plugins > > Capabilities, or with ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke <grant>. The kernel bumps the authorization epoch. Calls in flight return revoked. Pending requests that need the grant complete as failed(revoked). Contributions that need the grant are withdrawn, including decorations, grabs, routes and watches. The plugin receives deactivate(revoked) and is activated again with the reduced list. This re-activation is not counted as a failure.
  • Later grants. A grant that the user adds, or one that a plugin upgrade requests and the user accepts, bumps the epoch too. The plugin receives deactivate(granted) and is activated again with the new list.
  • Disable. A disabled plugin receives deactivate(disabled) and its contributions are withdrawn. See Lifecycle.

What the user sees

  • The review dialog at install, and the prompt for H capabilities at first activation of a T1 plugin.
  • Settings > Plugins > > Capabilities, which lists each grant with its state.
  • ilium plugin grants <id>, which also shows declined grants.
  • ilium plugin logs <id>, which shows each refusal, each file write outside data and cache, each process run with its arguments, and each clipboard read by length only.

Errors

Manifest errors are reported as error lines by ilium plugin install and ilium plugin build, one line per error.

Code Cause
manifest.grant-unknown The name is not a capability of this plugin API version.
manifest.grant-argument The grant has an argument, but the name takes none.
manifest.grant-argument-missing The name needs an argument and none was given.
manifest.grant-wildcard A wildcard was used where the name does not accept one, such as process.run:*.
manifest.grant-scope The file scope is unknown or does not accept that access.
manifest.grant-side The capability is not available on the side that requests it.
manifest.grant-tier The capability is for bundled plugins only.
manifest.grant-dependency The capability also needs another capability.
manifest.export-grant An export needs a capability that the manifest does not request.

Runtime codes that relate to grants are not-permitted (the capability is declined, revoked in flight, or the argument is outside the grant), revoked (the authorization epoch changed during the call) and failed(revoked) (a pending request lost its grant).

Edge cases to design for:

  • fs.pick needs fs.read:picked or fs.write:picked. Without either it fails with manifest.grant-dependency.
  • settings.write-all needs settings.read-all, and the review dialog cannot grant write alone.
  • settings.contribute:<tab-id> lets a plugin add sections to one built-in tab, such as settings.contribute:terminal. It is normal risk and independent of settings.read-all and settings.write-all: it never implies them, and they never imply it. A plugin's own tabs need no grant. See Plugin settings extension.
  • fs.write:agent-sessions:<agent> is refused at install with manifest.grant-scope. Transcripts are read only.
  • An inference-provider export needs inference.provide. Without the grant the plugin installs but is never selected as a provider.
  • A process.run call for a program outside its grant fails with invalid-argument before the process starts. A cwd that the plugin cannot read is not-permitted.
  • A http:* grant, or any other bare wildcard, is refused. A redirect follows the same host rule on each hop.

Migration of animation rights

Earlier animation packages used a separate set of rights. The new names replace them. network.http becomes http:<host>, audio.microphone becomes audio.capture, state.persist becomes the always-granted storage, and input.pointer becomes the scene's wants-pointer. Animation packages must be rebuilt, because there is no compatibility layer.
